PHASE 7 · FNP CERTIFICATION REVIEW & CLINICAL INTEGRATION

Week 154 — Lesson 178: Psychiatric, Behavioral & Substance Use Clinical Integration Board Review

FNP-level goal: Integrate symptom course, mental status, medical and medication causes, suicide and violence risk, substance exposure, life stage, function, capacity, and social context to distinguish outpatient syndromes from behavioral health emergencies and deliver collaborative, recovery-oriented care.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate depression, bipolar disorder, anxiety, trauma-related illness, psychosis, delirium, neurocognitive disorder, substance effects, and medical mimics.
  • Conduct a structured suicide assessment after a positive screen or concerning presentation and select a safe disposition.
  • Recognize mania, severe psychosis, catatonia, serotonin toxicity, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, severe eating-disorder instability, overdose, and dangerous withdrawal.
  • Apply measurement-based follow-up, medication safety, psychotherapy referral, collaborative care, and shared decisions.
  • Identify opioid, alcohol, sedative, stimulant, cannabis, and other substance-use disorders without stigma and offer evidence-based treatment.
  • Use safety planning, lethal-means counseling, crisis resources, confidentiality, and explicit follow-up ownership to close care gaps.

Part 1 — The MIND-SAFETY Framework

Psychiatric symptoms can arise from primary mental illness, substance intoxication or withdrawal, medication, endocrine or neurologic disease, infection, sleep deprivation, trauma, or social crisis. Diagnosis begins with safety and time course—not with a questionnaire score alone.

  • M — Medical stability first: vital signs, glucose, oxygenation, neurologic findings, pregnancy, toxidrome, and delirium.
  • I — Identify immediate risk: suicide, violence, inability to care for self, abuse, intoxication, withdrawal, or unsafe environment.
  • N — Name the syndrome and tempo: episodic, persistent, fluctuating, psychotic, manic, trauma-related, or substance-linked.
  • D — Define differential and drivers: medications, substances, sleep, pain, endocrine, neurologic, infectious, and psychosocial causes.
  • S — Screen with purpose: use validated tools to open assessment, not replace it.
  • A — Assess function and capacity: work, relationships, self-care, cognition, judgment, and decision-specific capacity.
  • F — Formulate risk and protective factors: current thoughts, intent, plan, access, past behavior, supports, and reasons for living.
  • E — Establish collaborative treatment: psychotherapy, medication, substance treatment, social support, and medical care.
  • TY — Track and yield to a safer level of care: arrange follow-up, own results, and escalate when outpatient care cannot contain risk.

Part 2 — First Decision: Medical or Behavioral Emergency?

Emergency findings include altered consciousness, severe agitation with hyperthermia, seizure, rigidity, autonomic instability, severe intoxication, respiratory depression, delirium, acute neurologic deficit, catatonia with medical compromise, inability to eat or drink, hemodynamic instability from an eating disorder, imminent suicide or violence risk, or inability to maintain basic safety.

Check glucose, oxygenation, temperature, vital signs, neurologic status, medication and substance exposure, pregnancy when relevant, and collateral history. A patient with psychiatric history can still have sepsis, stroke, hypoglycemia, thyroid disease, medication toxicity, or head injury.

Part 3 — The Mental Status Examination

Document appearance and behavior, psychomotor activity, speech, mood, affect, thought process, thought content, perception, cognition, insight, judgment, impulse control, and reliability. Describe observations rather than labels: “speech rapid and difficult to interrupt” is more useful than “manic-looking.”

Assess orientation, attention, memory, abstraction, and executive function as indicated. Attention that fluctuates or cannot be sustained suggests delirium more than an isolated mood disorder.

Part 4 — Build the Timeline

Ask when the patient was last at baseline, whether onset was sudden or gradual, whether symptoms fluctuate, prior episodes, sleep change, seasonality, pregnancy or postpartum timing, trauma, bereavement, medication changes, substances, and functional decline.

Episodic mood elevation changes the interpretation of depression. Symptoms occurring only during intoxication or withdrawal may be substance-induced. Abrupt late-life psychiatric change raises concern for medical, neurologic, medication, or neurocognitive disease.

Part 5 — Major Depression

Major depressive episodes involve persistent depressed mood or loss of interest with associated changes in sleep, energy, concentration, appetite, psychomotor activity, guilt or worthlessness, and thoughts of death, causing distress or impairment. Grief and depression can coexist; context does not eliminate illness.

Assess bipolar history before antidepressant monotherapy, along with substances, thyroid disease, anemia, sleep apnea, pain, medications, pregnancy, and safety. Treatment includes psychotherapy, medication when appropriate, exercise and sleep support, social interventions, and measurement-based follow-up.

Part 6 — Screening Is Not Diagnosis

Validated tools such as PHQ-9 or GAD-7 can measure symptoms and response, but scores do not establish etiology, rule out bipolar disorder, determine capacity, or independently classify suicide risk.

A positive suicide item requires direct assessment. A low score does not override observed psychosis, intoxication, severe functional decline, or a credible collateral report.

Part 7 — Bipolar Disorder and Mania

Mania involves a distinct period of abnormally elevated, expansive, or irritable mood with increased energy plus symptoms such as decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, racing thoughts, grandiosity, distractibility, and risky activity, with marked impairment, hospitalization, or psychosis. Hypomania is less impairing and lacks psychosis.

Ask every depressed patient about prior periods of reduced need for sleep and increased activation. Antidepressant treatment without recognizing bipolar disorder can destabilize selected patients. Acute mania with psychosis, dangerous behavior, exhaustion, or inability to care for self requires urgent psychiatric care.

Part 8 — Anxiety Disorders

Generalized anxiety involves excessive difficult-to-control worry across domains with physical and cognitive symptoms. Panic attacks are abrupt surges of fear with autonomic symptoms; panic disorder requires recurrent unexpected attacks and persistent concern or behavior change. Social anxiety, specific phobia, and illness anxiety have different triggers.

Evaluate arrhythmia, thyroid disease, asthma, hypoglycemia, stimulant or caffeine exposure, medication effects, withdrawal, and trauma. Avoid reinforcing endless medical testing when a coherent anxiety diagnosis exists, but do not use anxiety to dismiss new red flags.

Part 9 — Trauma-Related Disorders

PTSD includes trauma exposure followed by intrusion, avoidance, negative cognition or mood, and arousal or reactivity symptoms lasting beyond the acute period with impairment. Ask permission before details and focus on symptoms, safety, and function rather than forcing a full trauma narrative.

Trauma-focused psychotherapy is central. Review sleep, nightmares, substances, dissociation, depression, suicide risk, pain, and medical mistrust. Benzodiazepines can worsen avoidance, dependence, and safety in some patients and are not a primary PTSD treatment.

Part 10 — Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder

Obsessions are intrusive unwanted thoughts or urges; compulsions are repetitive behaviors or mental acts used to reduce distress. Insight varies. Distinguish OCD from generalized worry, psychosis, rigid personality traits, tics, and culturally normative rituals.

Exposure and response prevention is a key psychotherapy. Medication often requires adequate duration and dosing, with specialist care for severe, treatment-resistant, or disabling disease.

Part 11 — Psychosis

Psychosis includes delusions, hallucinations, disorganized thought or behavior, and negative symptoms. Determine onset, substances, medications, mood episodes, neurologic findings, delirium, trauma, and functional decline.

First-episode psychosis, postpartum psychosis, command hallucinations, severe agitation, catatonia, inability to eat or drink, or dangerous behavior requires urgent specialty evaluation. Do not assume all hallucinations equal schizophrenia.

Part 12 — Delirium vs Dementia vs Depression

Delirium is acute and fluctuating with impaired attention and awareness, often caused by infection, medication, withdrawal, metabolic disturbance, pain, urinary retention, constipation, or environmental change. Dementia is usually chronic and progressive. Depression can impair concentration and memory but does not typically produce fluctuating inattention.

Delirium is a medical emergency until the cause is found. Treat the driver, reduce deliriogenic medications, support sleep and orientation, mobilize, and use antipsychotics only for selected severe safety situations—not to normalize a score.

Part 13 — Suicide Screening and Assessment

Ask directly and calmly about passive death wishes, suicidal thoughts, method, plan, intent, preparatory behavior, recent escalation, and past attempts. Assess access to firearms, medications, or other lethal means; intoxication; agitation; psychosis; recent loss; pain; legal or financial crisis; and ability to collaborate.

Protective factors—relationships, beliefs, responsibilities, coping, treatment engagement—matter but do not cancel acute intent or access. Risk formulation is a clinical synthesis, not a simple low-medium-high score generated by one tool.

Part 14 — Acute Suicide Disposition

Current intent, a feasible plan, access to lethal means, recent attempt or rehearsal, severe intoxication, command hallucinations, inability to collaborate, or lack of a safe setting generally requires immediate crisis or emergency evaluation and continuous safety support.

Do not leave a high-risk patient alone or send the patient to drive independently. Follow local emergency and involuntary-evaluation law. In the United States, call or text 988 for crisis support; use 911 or emergency services when immediate life-threatening danger requires rapid response.

Part 15 — Safety Planning

A collaborative safety plan identifies personal warning signs, internal coping strategies, people and places for distraction, trusted contacts, professionals and crisis resources, and concrete steps to make the environment safer. It should be accessible during a crisis and rehearsed when possible.

A “no-suicide contract” is not a safety plan and does not establish safety. Include lethal-means counseling with respectful temporary separation from firearms, excess medications, or other identified methods. Arrange rapid follow-up and proactive contact after acute risk.

Part 16 — Violence Risk

Assess specific threats, target, intent, plan, access to weapons, past violence, escalating agitation, intoxication, paranoia, command hallucinations, and protective controls. Separate anger from imminent violence while taking credible threats seriously.

Follow jurisdictional duties to protect or warn, emergency law, and workplace safety procedures. Avoid interviewing a severely agitated armed patient without support.

Part 17 — Capacity and Informed Refusal

Decision-making capacity is specific to the decision and time. The patient must communicate a choice, understand relevant information, appreciate consequences in personal context, and reason about options. Psychiatric diagnosis alone does not remove capacity.

Address reversible barriers such as delirium, intoxication, language, hearing, pain, or inadequate explanation. If capacity is absent, identify the legally authorized surrogate and provide emergency treatment under applicable standards when delay threatens life.

Part 18 — Antidepressant Selection and Monitoring

Choose treatment from diagnosis, prior response, target symptoms, adverse effects, interactions, pregnancy, sexual effects, bleeding risk, seizure risk, cardiac disease, overdose toxicity, and patient preference. Explain that benefit is delayed while some adverse effects begin earlier.

Monitor activation, emerging mania, akathisia, sleep, adherence, suicide risk, and functional response early in treatment and after dose changes. Do not stop certain antidepressants abruptly because discontinuation symptoms can mimic relapse or illness.

Part 19 — Serotonin Toxicity

Serotonin toxicity can follow serotonergic combinations or overdose and typically involves mental-status change, autonomic activation, and neuromuscular hyperactivity such as clonus and hyperreflexia. Onset is often rapid.

Stop serotonergic agents and arrange urgent care based on severity. Distinguish from neuroleptic malignant syndrome, anticholinergic toxicity, sepsis, and malignant hyperthermia.

Part 20 — Antipsychotic Safety

Monitor weight, waist or metabolic risk, blood pressure, glucose, lipids, movement disorders, prolactin effects, sedation, orthostasis, QT risk, and drug interactions. Shared decisions should acknowledge both symptom benefit and long-term burden.

High fever, severe rigidity, altered mental status, and autonomic instability after dopamine-blocking exposure suggest neuroleptic malignant syndrome and require emergency care. Acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, and tardive dyskinesia require distinct responses.

Part 21 — Mood Stabilizers

Lithium requires kidney, thyroid, calcium, pregnancy, hydration, interaction, and serum-level monitoring. Toxicity can be precipitated by dehydration, kidney injury, NSAIDs, selected diuretics, and RAAS-active medicines. Tremor, vomiting, ataxia, confusion, or worsening neurologic symptoms require urgent evaluation.

Valproate, carbamazepine, and lamotrigine have different hepatic, hematologic, dermatologic, interaction, and reproductive risks. Avoid treating all mood stabilizers as interchangeable.

Part 22 — Insomnia

Insomnia assessment includes schedule, duration, sleep opportunity, substances, medications, mood, mania, anxiety, pain, restless legs, circadian pattern, and obstructive sleep apnea. Chronic insomnia is not simply a deficiency of sedative medication.

Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia is first-line for chronic insomnia. Sedatives can worsen falls, cognition, respiratory risk, tolerance, and dependence. A markedly reduced need for sleep with increased energy suggests mania rather than primary insomnia.

Part 23 — Eating Disorders

Eating disorders can occur at any body size. Ask about restriction, bingeing, vomiting, laxatives, compulsive exercise, body image, weight trajectory, menstrual or endocrine effects, syncope, chest symptoms, and suicidality.

Bradycardia, hypotension, orthostasis, hypothermia, severe electrolyte disturbance, arrhythmia, dehydration, acute food refusal, or suicidality may require medical stabilization. Refeeding can cause dangerous electrolyte shifts and requires coordinated care.

Part 24 — Substance Use: Ask Without Stigma

Ask what substance, amount, route, frequency, last use, tolerance, withdrawal, overdose, impaired control, consequences, prior treatment, and recovery goals. Include alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, opioids, stimulants, sedatives, hallucinogens, inhalants, and nonmedical prescription use.

Use person-first language and distinguish use, risky use, physical dependence, and substance-use disorder. A positive screen should lead to assessment and options—not punishment or abandonment.

Part 25 — Alcohol Use Disorder and Withdrawal

Alcohol use disorder is defined by impaired control and consequences, not one laboratory value. Offer behavioral treatment and evidence-based medications when appropriate while assessing liver, kidney, opioid, pregnancy, and adherence factors.

Withdrawal can begin after reduction and progress from tremor, anxiety, sweating, and tachycardia to seizure or delirium. Prior complicated withdrawal, heavy sustained use, major comorbidity, pregnancy, unstable housing, or current severe symptoms increases the need for monitored treatment.

Part 26 — Sedative-Hypnotic Withdrawal

Benzodiazepine and other sedative withdrawal can cause anxiety, insomnia, autonomic symptoms, perceptual disturbance, seizure, and delirium. Abrupt discontinuation after sustained exposure can be dangerous.

Review all prescribers and formulations. Coordinate an individualized gradual taper when appropriate; severe withdrawal or high-risk polysubstance use needs medically supervised care.

Part 27 — Opioid Overdose

Opioid overdose produces depressed consciousness, slow or absent breathing, and often miosis, although pupils are not definitive. Call emergency services, support ventilation, administer naloxone, and repeat according to product and protocol because potent or long-acting opioids may outlast naloxone.

After reversal, monitor for recurrent toxicity and connect the patient to OUD treatment. Overdose is a sentinel event, not a moral failure.

Part 28 — Opioid Use Disorder and MOUD

Buprenorphine, methadone, and naltrexone are FDA-approved medications for OUD. Medication reduces withdrawal, craving, illicit use, and overdose risk; counseling and recovery supports should be available but should not become unnecessary barriers to medication.

Assess opioid type, last use, withdrawal, fentanyl exposure, overdose history, pregnancy, pain, other sedatives, and treatment preference. Offer naloxone to the patient and likely responders and teach overdose response. Federal waiver requirements for buprenorphine prescribing were removed, although clinicians must follow current federal and state rules.

Part 29 — Stimulants

Stimulant intoxication can cause agitation, paranoia, chest pain, severe hypertension, hyperthermia, seizure, rhabdomyolysis, or stroke. Emergency symptoms require medical treatment, not psychiatric clearance alone.

Withdrawal often involves fatigue, sleep change, depression, and craving; suicide risk may rise. Evidence-based treatment emphasizes contingency management and behavioral care while addressing cardiovascular, dental, infectious, and psychiatric complications.

Part 30 — Cannabis and Other Substances

Cannabis can contribute to impaired driving, panic, psychosis risk, cyclic vomiting, and use disorder. Persistent vomiting relieved by hot bathing suggests cannabinoid hyperemesis but does not exclude pregnancy, obstruction, metabolic disease, or other causes.

Ask about high-potency products, vaping, edibles, synthetic cannabinoids, and co-use. Hallucinogens, inhalants, kratom, and novel products require poison-control or toxicology resources when presentation is uncertain.

Part 31 — Tobacco and Nicotine

Assess cigarettes, vaping, smokeless tobacco, nicotine pouches, readiness, and prior quit attempts. Combine behavioral support with FDA-approved pharmacotherapy when appropriate. Repeated offers are more effective than judgment.

Pregnancy, cardiovascular disease, psychiatric illness, and adolescents require tailored counseling, but these groups should not be denied cessation support.

Part 32 — Perinatal Mental Health

Screen during pregnancy and postpartum with systems for diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up. Depression and anxiety can affect attachment, function, sleep, safety, and infant care. Medication decisions balance fetal or infant exposure against untreated illness.

Postpartum psychosis—confusion, delusions, hallucinations, severe insomnia, mania, or disorganized behavior—is an emergency with suicide and infant-harm risk. Do not manage it as routine “baby blues.”

Part 33 — Children and Adolescents

Presentations may include irritability, school decline, somatic symptoms, behavior change, sleep disturbance, substance use, self-harm, or family conflict. Obtain confidential developmentally appropriate history while involving caregivers safely.

Assess bullying, trauma, abuse, eating disorder, ADHD, learning disorder, mood, anxiety, psychosis, substances, online risk, firearm access, and suicide. Treatment should integrate family, school, therapy, medical causes, and medication monitoring.

Part 34 — Older Adults

New anxiety, depression, hallucinations, or behavior change may reflect delirium, neurocognitive disorder, sensory loss, medication, pain, isolation, grief, sleep disorder, substance use, or elder mistreatment. Polypharmacy increases falls and cognitive risk.

Suicide risk remains important in later life, particularly with loss, pain, disability, isolation, and firearm access. Ask directly rather than assuming older adults will volunteer thoughts.

Part 35 — Collaborative Care and Follow-Up

Effective primary-care behavioral health uses a shared treatment plan, measurement, psychotherapy access, medication management, care coordination, and psychiatric consultation when needed. Define the target symptom and functional outcome before treatment.

Early follow-up is especially important after treatment initiation, hospital discharge, overdose, withdrawal, suicide crisis, or medication change. “Referral placed” is not closure; confirm connection and manage risk during the wait.

Part 36 — Board-Style Case 1: Suicide Risk

A patient with worsening depression reports intent to shoot himself tonight, has a loaded firearm at home, and cannot identify a safe person or plan.

Reasoning: Current intent, specific method, immediate access, and inability to collaborate indicate acute high risk. Maintain safety, do not leave the patient alone, and arrange emergency crisis evaluation. A no-suicide promise is inadequate.

Part 37 — Board-Style Case 2: Mania

A patient sleeps two hours nightly without fatigue, speaks rapidly, has grandiose business plans, spends recklessly, and becomes threatening when challenged.

Reasoning: Reduced need for sleep, activation, grandiosity, risky behavior, and major impairment suggest mania. Assess substances and medical causes while arranging urgent psychiatric care; antidepressant monotherapy is not the next step.

Part 38 — Board-Style Case 3: Delirium

An older adult with a urinary catheter becomes acutely inattentive, disoriented, and visually hallucinatory, with symptoms fluctuating through the day.

Reasoning: Acute fluctuation and impaired attention indicate delirium. Search for infection, medications, retention, metabolic disturbance, pain, and other causes rather than diagnosing a new primary psychotic disorder.

Part 39 — Board-Style Case 4: Opioid Overdose

A person is unresponsive with respirations 4/min after suspected fentanyl use.

Reasoning: Support ventilation, call emergency services, administer naloxone, and monitor for recurrent toxicity. After stabilization, offer MOUD linkage and naloxone access without stigma.

Part 40 — Board-Style Case 5: Postpartum Psychosis

Six days postpartum, a patient has not slept, says the infant is possessed, hears commands, and behaves unpredictably.

Reasoning: This is postpartum psychosis with immediate parent and infant safety risk. Arrange emergency psychiatric and medical care; routine outpatient antidepressant follow-up is unsafe.

Part 41 — Common Board Traps

  • Trap: A screening score is the diagnosis. Correction: tools support but do not replace differential diagnosis, safety assessment, or function.
  • Trap: Asking about suicide causes suicide. Correction: direct respectful assessment is necessary for safety.
  • Trap: A safety contract protects the patient. Correction: use collaborative safety planning, lethal-means counseling, and appropriate disposition.
  • Trap: Every depression receives an antidepressant immediately. Correction: screen for bipolar disorder, substances, medical mimics, and safety.
  • Trap: Counseling must precede MOUD. Correction: counseling should be offered, but unnecessary barriers to effective medication can increase harm.
  • Trap: Psychiatric history explains acute confusion. Correction: acute fluctuating inattention is delirium until a medical cause is addressed.

Part 42 — Final Board-Ready Algorithm

  1. Stabilize medically: assess vital signs, glucose, oxygenation, neurologic status, intoxication, withdrawal, pregnancy, and toxidromes.
  2. Assess immediate safety: suicide, violence, self-care, abuse, weapons, overdose, and environment.
  3. Build the timeline and syndrome: mood, anxiety, psychosis, cognition, trauma, sleep, function, and substance relationship.
  4. Rule in or out drivers: medicines, substances, endocrine, neurologic, infectious, metabolic, pain, and social crisis.
  5. Treat collaboratively: psychotherapy, medication, MOUD, harm reduction, social support, and medical care.
  6. Select disposition: emergency, crisis stabilization, urgent specialty, collaborative primary care, or routine follow-up.
  7. Close the loop: safety plan, lethal-means counseling, crisis contacts, early reassessment, and verified referral connection.

High-Yield Summary

  • Medical instability, delirium, overdose, withdrawal, and toxidromes must be addressed before psychiatric labeling.
  • Screening instruments measure symptoms; they do not independently establish diagnosis or safety.
  • Assess bipolar history before antidepressant monotherapy in depression.
  • Suicide assessment includes current thoughts, intent, plan, access, past behavior, intoxication, supports, and ability to collaborate.
  • Safety planning and lethal-means counseling are active interventions; a no-suicide contract is not.
  • Alcohol or sedative withdrawal, serotonin toxicity, NMS, postpartum psychosis, and severe eating-disorder instability can be emergencies.
  • Buprenorphine, methadone, and naltrexone are evidence-based OUD treatments; naloxone access saves lives.
  • Every crisis discharge, medication change, referral, overdose, and positive screen needs explicit follow-up ownership.

Clinical note: This lesson is educational. Apply current VA/DoD, SAMHSA, CDC, FDA, local behavioral-health crisis pathways, state law, prescribing regulations, and patient-specific specialist collaboration. In the United States, call or text 988 for crisis support; call emergency services for immediate life-threatening danger.
